SO, WHEN ANTIBIOTICS ARE USED, THEY KILL MOST OF THE BACTERIA. BUT SOME BACTERIA MAY HAVE NATURAL VARIATIONS THAT MAKE THEM RESISTANT. THESE RESISTANT BACTERIA SURVIVE THE TREATMENT AND REPRODUCE, PASSING ON THEIR RESISTANT GENES TO THEIR OFFSPRING. OVER TIME, THIS LEADS TO A POPULATION OF BACTERIA THAT IS RESISTANT TO THE ANTIBIOTIC.

NOW, OVERPRESCRIPTION OF ANTIBIOTICS ACCELERATES THIS PROCESS. I NEED TO MAKE SURE I CONNECT THE EVOLUTIONARY ASPECT WITH THE OVERPRESCRIPTION PART. OVERPRESCRIPTION INCREASES THE FREQUENCY OF THIS SELECTIVE PRESSURE, THUS SPEEDING UP THE EVOLUTION OF RESISTANCE.

I SHOULD ALSO CHECK IF THERE ARE OTHER FACTORS, LIKE GENETIC TRANSFER OF RESISTANCE GENES BETWEEN BACTERIA (HORIZONTAL GENE TRANSFER), WHICH CAN SPREAD RESISTANCE MORE RAPIDLY. THIS ADDS ANOTHER LAYER TO THE EVOLUTIONARY MECHANISM.

final_answer:
antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, an evolutionary mechanism. when antibiotics are used, they kill susceptible bacteria, but some bacteria may have genetic mutations that confer resistance. these resistant bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on their resistance genes to offspring. over time, resistant strains become more common in the population. 

overprescription accelerates this process by frequently exposing bacteria to antibiotics, acting as a selective pressure. each use of antibiotics kills non-resistant bacteria, allowing resistant strains to thrive and multiply. this repeated exposure increases the likelihood of resistance genes spreading through horizontal gene transfer (e.g., plasmid exchange) and reduces the effectiveness of antibiotics. misuse in healthcare, agriculture, or self-medication intensifies this selective pressure, speeding up the evolution of resistance.
